items.title: A new font promises to hide your text from AI.
items.excerpt: Design and tech company Mixfont released Decoy Font, a typeface humans can read but large language models and AI crawlers cannot parse — pitched at writers and publishers who want their text online but out of training sets.
items.note: Concrete tool with a typography/craft hook; sits exactly at the design x books intersection. Freshest item in the pool.

items.title: Pangram Has Emerged as the Gold Standard of AI Detection. Should You Trust It?
items.excerpt: WIRED profiles Pangram, the AI-detection tool publishers, editors and journalists now lean on to vet manuscripts. "Meet the AI police who can make or break careers—in publishing and beyond."
items.note: Workflow-level: detection scores are becoming a gate in acquisition and editing. Pairs with the-decoder item — curator should pick one.

items.title: Pangram's biggest flaw is users turning its scores into public shaming
items.excerpt: Pangram only somewhat reliably measures whether AI was used, yet its scores are being weaponized on social media to accuse writers of not doing their own thinking — a gap between measurement and judgement.
items.note: Same subject as the WIRED piece but a different angle (the social consequence of scores). Dedupe against #2.

items.title: Claude Fable 5.1 decoded a centuries-old royalist message hidden in plain sight since 1653
items.excerpt: Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.1 appears to have cracked a 1653 number puzzle researchers had left unsolved, a concrete case of a frontier model working on historical text and archival scholarship.
items.note: Archive/manuscript angle rather than tooling; useful if the curator wants a non-policy, non-detection card.

items.title: We Can Now Track AI-generated Content. It Doesn't Solve the Real Problem.
items.excerpt: Identifying AI content is now embedded in Claude models. The post argues provenance signals don't answer the question publishers actually have — and create new ones for editorial workflows.
items.note: Adjacent to the 08-29 watermarking card already run; keep only if the curator wants the publisher-workflow read rather than the vendor news.

items.title: Second annual AI survey by Gotham Ghostwriters and Bernoff.com
items.excerpt: The second annual survey of working writers and editors is underway, rebuilt to reflect the AI tools and disclosure problems that appeared in the past year of ghostwriting and book work.
items.note: Ghostwriting/day-4 emphasis. Generic og:image — ax-media should pull an in-body image or generate.

items.title: The Art of Wandering: Protecting Creative Taste in the Age of Algorithms
items.excerpt: Novelist Kyla Zhao on how recommendation systems and AI-smoothed inputs narrow a writer's taste, and the deliberate wandering habits she uses to keep her own reading and drafting unpredictable.
items.note: Craft-side counterweight to the tooling cards; concrete practice, not a think-piece about the industry.

items.title: "번역, 숙고 속 만들어" "AI 진출 막기 어려워"
items.excerpt: '딸깍 출판'에 이어 '딸깍 번역'이 화두가 된 한국 출판계. AI 번역을 고지 없이 쓴 고전문학 앱 '책도둑'이 7월 서비스를 중단한 뒤, 번역가와 출판인들이 AI 활용 표시 기준을 놓고 부딪힌다.
items.note: Korean translation-and-disclosure debate. Near-neighbour of the 09-02 khan card (same paper, same day, different piece) — dedupe carefully. og:image is a logo; ax-media must find a real visual.

items.title: 서울iT아카데미 홍대, AI 디지털 출판콘텐츠 인재 양성
items.excerpt: 원고 교정·교열과 편집디자인 중심이던 출판편집 직무가 AI 자료조사·원고 분석·전자책/오디오북 제작으로 재편되면서, 국내 교육과정이 생성형 AI 활용 역량을 전제로 다시 짜이고 있다.
items.note: Lowest-priority in the pool: promotional in tone. Useful only as evidence of how the Korean editorial job description itself is being rewritten.

items.title: Read These Books Before You Enter the AI Debates
items.excerpt: A reading list of nonfiction on AI and social media aimed at readers who want their opinions grounded in reporting rather than discourse.
items.note: Weakest design-relevance of the pool (curation, not craft or tooling). Include only if a lighter card is needed.

items.title: How To Redesign Your Author Business For The Environment That Actually Exists, With Tracy Cooper-Posey
items.excerpt: Joanna Penn's episode opens with a 'Perspectives on AI in writing' segment before Tracy Cooper-Posey's 'solar sail' theory of choosing which author-marketing efforts still reach readers in ten years.
items.note: Social/YouTube slot for day 4 (Creative Penn). uploadDate verified from the watch page JSON-LD; AI content is a segment, not the whole episode.
